newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia retail weakness a threat to growth record.
newsitem.headline: Australia retail weakness a threat to growth record.

text.p: Australian economic data on Tuesday confirmed an unhappy Christmas for the nation's retailers and suggested a record growth run may be at an end, but analysts said they did not expect an interest rate cut soon.
The data backed up anecdotal evidence of poor Christmas sales, showing a 1.0 percent fall in December retail trade.
"This confirms the story that both retailers and other business related to the industry have been telling us," said National Australia Bank senior economist Tim Pfitzner.
Market forecasts had centred on a 0.5 percent rise for the month. The retail data series has fallen in each of the last five months, an unmatched downturn in its 35-year history.
More importantly, real retail trade fell 1.3 percent over the December quarter, well below the median market forecast for a 0.5 percent fall and the largest quarterly fall since June 1983.
The calculation for real retail trade removes price effects from the data and gives an indication of the volumes of goods sold.
The quarterly fall meant retail trade, which accounts for about a quarter of gross domestic product (GDP), will detract about 0.3 percentage points from December quarter GDP.
Some economists began to wind back their GDP forecasts after the retail figures were released.
Colonial State Bank revised down its forecast for December quarter GDP to flat.
The bank's chief economist Hans Kunnen said: "We would not rule out the possibility that economic growth contracted in the December quarter."
Economic growth has been positive for the past 21 quarters, dating back to the June quarter of 1991, the longest period of uninterrupted growth in the history of the GDP series.
However, some economists expressed doubts about the size of the monthly fall in retail trade, saying the seasonal adjustment process was not adequately capturing a change in spending patterns.
Since the recession in the early 1990s, shoppers appear to be delaying purchases until the post-Christmas clearance sales in January, so the numbers for that month could show a rebound, they said.

"The numbers suggest that, obviously, the consumer cut back spending...but because of the change in spending patterns, I wouldn't read too much into this," said Merrill Lynch Australia chief economist Nigel Douglas.

The retail figures were released as the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) held its first board meeting of 1997, but the data was seen as having little impact on their deliberations on monetary policy settings.
Rothschild Australia chief economist Ric Simes said the RBA had already considered the weakness in retailing when interest rates were cut in both November and December last year.
"They were expecting a weak period over Christmas and New Year and wanted to provide some stimulus, and take those measures as early as possible," he said.
Analysts said the bias was still towards a further rate cut, but it was more likely in March rather than February.
The RBA would have had more time to assess the impact of the three rate cuts in the second half of 1996, and would also be able to watch for any January rebound in retail trade, they said.
